strengths: The core idea is useful and reasonably original: UMF treats deterministic choices among heterogeneous masked-diffusion models or inference configurations as MCTS actions, enabling partial trajectories to be cached and reused. This is a meaningful extension beyond primarily stochastic token- or mask-level branching.

The coding results are promising and consistently favor UMF under the reported NFE accounting. At NFE 12,288, UMF obtains 28/88/72 Pass@1 on LiveCodeBench/HumanEval+/MBPP+, compared with 21/81/68 for multi-model AB-MCTS and 19/75/66 for the best-of-N model pair.

The ablations address relevant alternatives. In particular, multi-model UMF exceeds paired independent single-model UMFs by 4, 10, and 3 points across the three coding benchmarks, while caching raises LiveCodeBench performance from 26% to 28% at the largest budget.

Presentation is generally clear. The state/action formulation, algorithm, scaling curves, action ablations, and qualitative search-tree example make the proposed procedure understandable at a high level. The manuscript source was also visually inspected: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/97da030861744034bbc654181a261423/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

The impact statement appropriately identifies code-generation misuse, unsafe reward optimization, computational cost, and access disparities, and suggests sensible deployment safeguards. I found no unresolved research-ethics issue that independently prevents acceptance.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence lacks uncertainty estimates. Each coding benchmark is reduced to only 100 problems, but the sampled problem identifiers, sampling procedure, and seeds are not reported. Results therefore move in one-percentage-point increments, and no confidence intervals, paired significance tests, or repeated runs are provided. This is especially problematic for stochastic baselines and for conclusions based on differences of only 2–4 points.

The mathematical-reasoning evidence does not support the claimed generalization strongly. Only UMF is reported on a 105-problem MATH subset, with no best-of-N, DTS, AB-MCTS, single-model, or independent-pair baseline. The reported 11.43-point scaling gain therefore does not establish that UMF is preferable to simpler uses of the same inference budget.

The theoretical analysis is heuristic and overclaimed. Equation (1) compares an oracle per-state minimum with the best fixed kernel without showing that MCTS can identify those local minima; moreover, action-dependent transitions induce different state distributions. Likewise, zero rollout randomness only gives the exact reward of one fixed deterministic continuation, not an exact value for alternative downstream policies or evidence that the trajectory has low generation error.

There is an unresolved inconsistency around determinism and caching. The method defines every positive-temperature action as stochastic, yet Table 4 evaluates UMF action sets containing temperatures 0.5 and 1.0. It is unclear whether such state-action pairs are cached, whether caching freezes one random realization, and how the algorithm and NFE accounting change when transitions are not deterministic.

Cross-tokenizer model switching is insufficiently specified. Decoding partially masked segments and re-encoding them can change token counts and boundaries, but the paper does not explain how mask positions, sequence length, residual mask ratios, or already committed spans are aligned afterward. The assertion that no structural degradation was observed is not supported by a quantitative ablation.

NFE counts only MDLM forward passes. It excludes reward-model inference or test execution, tokenizer conversion, search overhead, and the memory cost of hosting two models; it also treats cached transitions as free. Consequently, the evidence supports efficiency under this particular accounting metric, but not the broader claims of compute or practical efficiency without FLOP, latency, memory, and end-to-end cost comparisons.

Search uses public or standard unit tests as rewards and selects the highest-scoring candidate. Evaluation on private or extended tests reduces direct leakage, but the method consequently assumes an informative executable reward oracle and may overfit sparse public tests. The number and provenance of reward tests and sensitivity to reward quality are not analyzed.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate: no code or artifact is identified, and important details such as benchmark subset IDs, prompts, random seeds, tie-breaking, exact DTS* modifications, reward and answer-extraction procedures, tokenizer conversion, and per-budget search behavior are missing. The paper also lacks a limitations discussion covering these evaluation and deployment assumptions. Overall, the idea and results merit further development, but these issues prevent others from reliably validating or building on the central claims.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely problem: inference-time scaling for masked diffusion language models. Treating model/configuration choice as an action in an unmasking search tree is intuitive and potentially useful.

The coding results are consistently favorable across LiveCodeBench, HumanEval+, and MBPP+. At NFE=12,288, UMF reports 28/88/72 Pass@1 versus 21/81/68 for the strongest listed AB-MCTS baseline. The independent two-model comparison in Table 5 is a useful attempt to separate trajectory-level collaboration from ordinary ensembling.

The paper evaluates several relevant alternatives, including Best-of-N, diffusion-specific tree search, adaptive-branching MCTS, randomized remasking, temperature variation, and independent allocation across two models. The cache ablation and action-type ablation also target important design choices.

Presentation is generally clear and visually polished. The algorithm, masking-ratio schedule, principal model settings, and NFE convention are described, and the appendix supplies broader scaling curves and formal definitions of the remasking strategies.

The impact statement appropriately discusses misuse of generated code, unsafe reward signals, computational cost, access disparities, inherited model biases, and practical mitigations. I found no unresolved research-ethics issue that independently warrants rejection.
weaknesses: Soundness: the empirical evidence is too small and statistically fragile for the central claims. Coding results use only 100 examples from each benchmark and MATH uses 105 sampled problems. The paper gives no confidence intervals, repeated trials, seed sensitivity, significance tests, or uncertainty over benchmark subsampling. Several reported differences are only a few examples, while the exact sampled instances are not identified.

Soundness: the evaluation uses public LiveCodeBench tests and the standard HumanEval/MBPP tests as search rewards, then selects the highest-reward candidate for evaluation on private or extended tests. This is closer to test-suite-guided program synthesis than general reasoning, and it gives an unusually informative verifier. The paper does not report performance with learned, noisy, sparse, or unavailable rewards on coding tasks, so the claim of broadly effective test-time scaling is insufficiently supported.

The theoretical analysis is weak. Equation 1 is an oracle inequality involving the unavailable true posterior and assumes selection of the locally best kernel; it neither shows that task reward tracks KL error nor that MCTS can identify those kernels. Likewise, a deterministic terminal rollout has zero sampling variance conditional on its state and action, but this observation does not establish that deterministic model switching is generally more sample-efficient or higher quality than stochastic search. The paper repeatedly describes the method as principled and attributes the gains to structural diversity more strongly than this analysis justifies.

Compute comparisons are incomplete. NFE treats a forward pass through different 7B/8B models as equal and excludes reward-model or test-execution cost, model residency/switching, tokenizer conversion, memory, and latency. Caching receives zero NFE cost, so conclusions about compute efficiency need wall-clock, FLOP, and memory measurements. The method also requires simultaneous access to multiple pretrained models, whereas many baselines use one; the pair baseline helps but does not fully normalize serving costs.

The heterogeneous-tokenizer mechanism is a major underspecified risk. Decoding and re-encoding a partially masked sequence can change token counts, boundaries, positions, and therefore the meaning of a fixed 768-token state and residual-mask schedule. The assertion that no structural degradation was observed is unsupported by measurements or an ablation. It is unclear how masks are aligned when lengths change, how cached states are canonicalized across tokenizers, and how generated-length constraints remain comparable.

Reproducibility is inadequate. There is no code or artifact reference, and the manuscript omits exact benchmark subsets and versions, prompts, seeds, tie-breaking and final-selection rules, detailed DTS*/AB-MCTS adaptations, action-selection ordering, cache keys, tokenizer-conversion pseudocode, hardware, runtime, and reward-computation details. Algorithm 1 also leaves important routines such as SELECTBEST and SELECTROLLOUTACTION undefined.

The novelty is incremental relative to the cited literature on diffusion tree search, MCTS decoding, and reward-aligned search. The main new element appears to be using heterogeneous pretrained MDLMs as deterministic tree actions plus caching. That could be a useful engineering contribution, but the paper does not adequately compare against or dissect the closest methods beyond adapted aggregate baselines.

The scope claims are overstated. Evidence outside code consists only of one scaling curve on a small MATH subset using a separate process-reward model, with no single-model or competing search baselines. This does not substantiate strong generalization to mathematical reasoning or reasoning tasks broadly.

The method description contains ambiguities that affect correctness: it uses the term “remasking” despite imposing monotonic unmasking; budget behavior when a rollout would exceed the remaining NFE is unspecified; cache retrieval semantics are unclear; and no analysis establishes whether improvements arise from MCTS, the hand-designed expansion schedule, deterministic exhaustive branching, or simply access to complementary models. Overall, the idea has merit, but the evidential and reproducibility weaknesses currently prevent reliable validation or adoption.

strengths: The paper introduces a useful and reasonably original test-time scaling approach for masked diffusion language models: heterogeneous models or inference configurations become deterministic MCTS actions, while intermediate rollout states are cached. This is well matched to the non-autoregressive unmasking process.

The coding results are consistently favorable under matched NFE budgets. At NFE=12,288, UMF reaches 28/88/72 Pass@1 on LiveCodeBench/HumanEval+/MBPP+, compared with 21/81/68 for multi-model AB-MCTS and 19/75/66 for paired Best-of-N. The margins are substantial on two of the three benchmarks.

The experiments include meaningful comparisons against Best-of-N, DTS*, and AB-MCTS, alongside ablations of caching, action type, and independent versus interleaved multi-model inference. In particular, the paired single-model UMF comparison supports the claim that interleaving models contributes beyond merely splitting compute between them.
The caching ablation provides concrete evidence for the proposed efficiency mechanism: at NFE=12,288, caching raises LiveCodeBench Pass@1 from 26% to 28%, with a reported 55.8% cache-hit rate.

The method and intuition are presented clearly, with helpful pseudocode, diagrams, scaling curves, and formal definitions of the remasking strategies. The discussion appropriately situates UMF relative to recent diffusion-specific search methods.

The impact statement identifies code-generation misuse, inference cost, access disparities, and inherited model risks, and recommends reasonable mitigations. No new human-subject or data-collection concerns are introduced.
weaknesses: The empirical samples are small and incompletely specified: only 100 problems from each coding benchmark and 105 sampled MATH problems are used, without problem identifiers, sampling procedure, repeated subsets, confidence intervals, or significance tests. With coding scores changing in one-percentage-point increments, several reported differences—especially on MBPP+ and in the caching ablation—may not be statistically reliable.

The MATH evidence does not support the broad comparative generalization claim. It reports only UMF as its NFE increases, on a small sampled subset, with no Best-of-N, DTS*, AB-MCTS, single-model, or independent-model baselines. It establishes scaling within UMF but not that UMF is preferable for mathematical reasoning.

The theoretical discussion is motivational rather than a sound performance analysis. Equation (1) assumes an oracle that selects the minimum-error kernel at every state; it does not show that MCTS with terminal task rewards discovers such a policy, nor connect accumulated KL error to benchmark correctness. Likewise, the assertion that one deterministic rollout gives the “exact value” of a branch conflates a deterministic realized terminal reward with the expected value relevant to broader solution quality.

The determinism argument is not fully consistent with the implementation. Dream uses temperature 0.1, while the paper's own definition makes every positive temperature stochastic; calling its transitions deterministic or claiming variance approximately zero requires quantitative validation. Caching a stochastic realization would also alter the effective search distribution.

NFE counts only model forward passes. The evaluation omits wall-clock latency, memory, reward-model/test-execution cost, tokenizer-conversion overhead, and the operational expense of maintaining two 7–8B models. Consequently, the efficiency and fixed-compute claims are narrower than the presentation suggests.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important details such as SELECTROLLOUTACTION, SELECTBEST, tie-breaking, precise node identity and cache keys, budget handling near termination, benchmark subsets, random seeds, reward aggregation, and the exact DTS* adaptation are not sufficiently specified, and no code or artifact availability statement is given.

The tokenizer-switching procedure is potentially consequential but is supported only by the statement that no structural degradation was observed. Re-encoding text can change sequence length, mask alignment, and position correspondence; quantitative diagnostics or an ablation are needed.

Originality is meaningful but incremental relative to DTS, MEDAL, TReASURe, and generic adaptive-branching MCTS. The principal novelty is the combination of heterogeneous deterministic actions and caching, rather than a fundamentally new search algorithm. Overall, the promising and sizable coding gains justify a weak accept, but the limited evaluation scale and under-specified methodology prevent a stronger rating.

strengths: Soundness: The core construction is intuitive: treating model/configuration choices as actions over partial unmasking states permits trajectory-level search and reuse of deterministic rollout prefixes. The cache ablation supports practical value, improving LiveCodeBench from 26% to 28% at 12,288 NFE.

Empirical scope: The paper evaluates three coding benchmarks, MATH, standard and block-diffusion decoding, two- and three-model action sets, several NFE budgets, and multiple search baselines. The reported coding improvements are consistent, including 28/88/72 for UMF versus 21/81/68 for multi-model AB-MCTS at 12,288 NFE.

Significance: Efficient test-time scaling for masked diffusion language models is timely, and model-interleaved decoding could be useful when heterogeneous pretrained MDLMs are available. Runtime, memory, cache-hit, and public-test-mismatch analyses add practical information.

Originality: Diffusion tree search itself is not new, but branching over heterogeneous pretrained models and exploiting the resulting reusable trajectories is a meaningful new combination relative to the cited DTS, MEDAL, and TReASURe approaches.

Presentation and ethics: The paper is generally well organized and visually clear. The impact statement appropriately discusses inference cost, unequal compute access, unsafe code generation, inherited model risks, and concrete deployment safeguards.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central deterministic-action justification is internally inconsistent. Dream/Dream-Coder actions use temperature 0.1, which the paper's own definition makes stochastic, yet Section 5 assumes approximately zero reward variance, Algorithm 1 caches state-action transitions as unique, and the conclusion claims strict determinism. No variance measurement, fixed-randomness definition, or sensitivity study establishes that temperature 0.1 is effectively deterministic.

The theoretical analysis does not substantiate UMF. Equation (1) compares pointwise minimum KL errors under an apparently shared state distribution, although the state distribution depends on prior action choices; moreover, MCTS observes terminal task rewards rather than the inaccessible local KL errors. Thus the inequality is motivational and does not imply that the proposed search finds a better switching policy.

Statistical evidence is insufficient. Each benchmark uses only 100 sampled coding problems (and 105 MATH problems), but problem identifiers, repeated trials, confidence intervals, paired tests, and uncertainty across stochastic baselines are absent. Several decisive margins are only 4–7 solved problems, so the evidence does not establish whether the improvements are robust rather than sampling or seed effects.

Reproducibility is weak: there is no code or artifact statement, seeds, sampled problem IDs, prompt templates, software versions, or complete implementation specification. SELECTROLLOUTACTION and SELECTBEST are undefined; DTS* modifications are unexplained; and cache keys, tie breaking, tokenizer conversion/truncation, PRM score aggregation, and handling of stochastic actions are not specified well enough to independently reproduce the method.

Compute matching by NFE is incomplete. A forward pass through different 7B/8B models is counted identically, while UMF additionally requires multiple models, tokenizer conversions, search, caching, and reward evaluation. The runtime table is useful, but no wall-clock- or hardware-matched baseline comparison establishes deployment-level efficiency.

The MATH evidence is limited: only UMF scaling appears in the main results, while the appendix comparison to TReASURe shows an unusually large gap (roughly 10% versus 59%) under acknowledged differences in reward interfaces and without enough implementation detail to make the comparison diagnostic.

Presentation omits important limitations. The paper should explicitly discuss dependence on a strong external verifier/reward, multiple resident models, small benchmark subsets, possible public-test overfitting, tokenizer-induced state changes, and the restricted evidence for domains beyond code and math. These omissions matter more than the otherwise adequate societal-impact discussion.

strengths: The core idea is intuitive and potentially useful: deterministic model/configuration choices provide diversity without token-level noise, while cached rollouts reuse previously computed model evaluations.
The experiments cover three coding benchmarks, sampled MATH problems, multiple compute budgets, action-set ablations, block diffusion, caching, runtime, verifier mismatch, and several baselines.
Some reported gains are meaningful: at 12,288 NFE, UMF obtains 28/88/72 on LiveCodeBench/HumanEval+/MBPP+, compared with 21/81/68 for multi-model AB-MCTS.
The paper is generally clear and organized, with readable pseudocode, definitions, figures, and deployment measurements.
Using heterogeneous pretrained MDLMs as deterministic tree-search actions is moderately original relative to prior diffusion tree-search work.
The impact statement appropriately discusses misuse, computational cost, access disparities, inherited model risks, and mitigations; no material research-ethics issue is apparent.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is statistically weak. Coding benchmarks are reduced to 100 problems and MATH to 105, with only point estimates and no confidence intervals, paired tests, repeated subsets, or seed variability. Many differences represent only 1–4 additional solved problems, and neither sampling indices nor the LiveCodeBench version/time window are specified.

The evaluation relies on privileged verifier feedback: public tests for LiveCodeBench and original standard tests for HumanEval/MBPP are used during search. This is not ordinary Pass@1 generation, and robustness to verifier overfitting is assessed only through one limited LiveCodeBench test-dropping experiment.

The theoretical analysis does not substantiate the method. Equation (1) is a generic sum-of-minima inequality; its inaccessible local KL errors are not optimized by UMF, action choices alter subsequent state distributions, and no connection to UCT's terminal verifier reward is established. Determinism gives the exact reward of one trajectory, not the expected value of an action under downstream choices.

The experiments do not isolate whether MCTS is necessary. There is no exhaustive, beam, random, or fixed-schedule search over the small action space, nor a simpler search using identical actions and caching. Improvements could therefore arise from model interleaving plus verifier selection rather than the proposed UCT procedure.

Comparisons with ReMDM and TReASURe are acknowledged to be non-drop-in. The extremely large MATH gap over TReASURe is insufficiently investigated and could reflect incompatible reward interfaces or implementation choices.

Reproducibility is inadequate: no code artifact is identified, and sampled problem IDs, prompt templates, model revisions, PRM scoring details, baseline hyperparameters, seeds, action ordering, tie-breaking, SELECTROLLOUTACTION/SELECTBEST behavior, and budget-boundary handling are omitted. The DTS* adaptation is also underspecified.

Cross-tokenizer state conversion is consequential but underdefined. Re-encoding generated spans can alter sequence lengths and alignment around masks; reporting 1.09% average length drift does not replace an exact conversion algorithm, truncation policy, or controlled artifact ablation.

NFE is an incomplete fairness metric across heterogeneous models and reward mechanisms: it treats different model forwards equally and excludes verifier/PRM costs. Runtime is reported only for UMF, preventing end-to-end efficiency comparisons with baselines.

The scientific limitations discussion omits central restrictions: dependence on multiple models and an informative external verifier, benchmark subsampling, test-time access to canonical tests, statistical uncertainty, and applicability when trustworthy rewards are unavailable. The idea is promising, but the current evidence and documentation are not reliable enough for acceptance.

strengths: Soundness: The main coding results are consistently favorable under matched NFE budgets. At NFE=12,288, UMF reaches 28.0/88.0/72.0 on LiveCodeBench/HumanEval+/MBPP+, compared with 21.0/81.0/68.0 for multi-model AB-MCTS and 19.0/75.0/66.0 for paired Best-of-N. Comparisons also include DTS*, ReMDM, TReASURe, multiple temperatures, and randomized-remasking variants.

The ablations meaningfully probe the proposed mechanism. The paper separates caching, action type, independent multi-model allocation, interleaved two-model generation, and a three-model action set. In particular, two-model UMF exceeds paired independent single-model UMFs, while cache removal lowers LiveCodeBench performance from 28.0 to 26.0 at NFE=12,288.

Significance and originality: Treating heterogeneous pretrained MDLMs or deterministic inference configurations as MCTS actions is a useful and moderately original exploration axis. Combining deterministic rollouts with trajectory caching is especially well suited to expensive diffusion decoding and may influence future inference-time scaling systems.

Presentation: The motivation, method, pseudocode, figures, and distinction from stochastic diffusion-tree methods are generally clear. The appendix adds block-diffusion results, runtime and memory measurements, verifier-mismatch tests, complete scaling curves, and formal remasking definitions.

The paper appropriately discusses inference cost, energy and access disparities, malicious code generation, inherited model risks, and practical safeguards. No unresolved human-subject or data-collection concern is apparent. weaknesses: The empirical samples are small—100 problems per coding benchmark and 105 MATH problems—and the paper reports neither confidence intervals nor significance tests. Several conclusions rest on differences of only a few solved problems, such as 28 versus 21 on LiveCodeBench or 72 versus 68 on MBPP+, so claims of significant or consistently superior performance are stronger than the statistical evidence establishes.

The MATH evidence is incomplete. The main scaling table reports only UMF, without corresponding single-model, paired-model, Best-of-N, or AB-MCTS results. The later TReASURe comparison is extremely unfavorable to that baseline but is acknowledged not to be a drop-in comparison. Consequently, broad generalization beyond code is only weakly supported.

The theoretical discussion is motivational rather than a sound guarantee. Equation (1) is a pointwise sum-of-minima inequality under a shared state distribution, whereas action choices alter subsequent state distributions; it therefore does not establish that an attainable switching policy has lower trajectory error. The text also says such a policy can 'strictly' outperform static models although the displayed inequality is non-strict. Likewise, a deterministic rollout gives one exact terminal reward for that rollout, not necessarily an exact action value when future decisions vary.

Compute matching by NFE ignores heterogeneous per-forward-pass cost, memory, and model-loading requirements. UMF keeps two models resident and uses 35.64 GiB on coding tasks, but baseline wall-clock and memory measurements are absent. Runtime comparisons are therefore insufficient to substantiate deployment-level efficiency, despite useful UMF-only profiling.

Search uses public or standard tests as rewards and selects candidates on those rewards. Private/extended tests reduce direct leakage, and the test-dropping ablation is helpful, but it does not quantify reward overfitting, false-positive selection, or performance without executable tests. This limits applicability to tasks lacking strong verifiers.

Reproducibility is not yet adequate for an Accept score: no code or artifact is identified; the exact sampled problem IDs, seeds, model revisions, baseline implementations, tie-breaking rules, action expansion order, and full selection/cache semantics are missing. Algorithm 1 leaves SELECTBEST and several caching details unspecified. These omissions make the extensive results difficult to independently reproduce.
